title: How a Spacecraft Catches a Space Station in 3.5 Hours
fb_caption: This week, a Chinese spacecraft docked with the Tiangong space station, carrying the first foreign astronaut ever to board it, an astronaut from Pakistan, and it got there about three and a half hours after liftoff. So how do you catch a target moving at about 17,000 miles an hour? Rewind the flight: a gentle nudge at docking, a chase from a lower and faster orbit, about ten minutes of rocket ride, and a liftoff timed for the moment the station's path passes overhead. Miss that window and the chase could take days instead of hours. Would you ride a rocket to a space station if you had the chance? Tell us below.

beats.text: This week, a Chinese spacecraft docked with the Tiangong space station, carrying the first foreign astronaut ever to board it, an astronaut from Pakistan. And it got there about three and a half hours after liftoff.
Three and a half hours, to catch a target moving at about seventeen thousand miles an hour. How? Rewind.

Seconds before contact, the two are lined up nose to port, and the gap is closing slower than you walk. A docking is usually a gentle nudge. Then latches grab hold, and pull the two together until they seal. Rewind again.

An hour or so earlier, the capsule is behind the station, and below it. Here's the trick: a lower orbit is a faster lap. So a chasing spacecraft usually stays low to catch up, then fires its engines to climb. Rewind further.
Roughly ten minutes after liftoff, the rocket's work is done. The capsule is in orbit, on its own.
And all the way back, to the launch pad. Because the real secret happens before the engines even light. Liftoff is timed for the moment the station's path passes overhead.
Miss that window, and the chase could take days instead of hours. Hit it, and computers can fly almost the whole pursuit on their own.
Takeaway: you can watch a space station yourself. Look for a bright, steady light, gliding across the sky just after sunset or before sunrise. Free tracking sites will tell you when.

items: JUST AFTER SUNSET OR BEFORE SUNRISE

beats.text: Would you ride a rocket to a space station if you had the chance? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who loves space. Because this week, a three-and-a-half-hour chase ended with a gentle nudge, and a first.
